subject: social
topic: A correction rarely catches the lie
angle: While corrections reduce the impact of misinformation, they often fail to eliminate it entirely, especially when the misinformation is implied, repeated, or negative.
title: The Persistence of Lies

hooks.text: Why does a correction not erase a lie?
You see a correction. The lie remains.
You trust the fact-check more than you should.
A headline, a correction, a lingering doubt.

reveal.headline: Corrections do not entirely eliminate the effect of misinformation.
reveal.body: Even after a debunking message is received, the initial impact of false information remains in the mind.

explain.headline: The type of lie changes how it sticks.
explain.body: Implied misinformation is more resistant to correction than explicit claims. Negative misinformation can also persist, sometimes causing more negative attitudes toward a subject after a correction is provided.

matters.headline: The correction is not a reset button.
matters.body: That may be why you still feel a lingering sense of doubt or distrust even after seeing a fact-check. The first impression leaves a mark that a simple correction cannot fully erase.

example.headline: The news feed at dinner.
example.body: You read a headline about a hospital. You see a correction later that evening. You still feel a sense of unease when you think about the building the next day.

question.headline: What lies do you still believe after you see the truth?

stat.label: the remaining effect of misinformation after correction

claims.text: A detailed debunking message is linked to both a debunking effect and a misinformation-persistence effect.
claims.quote: Surprisingly, however, a detailed debunking message also correlated positively with the misinformation-persistence effect.

claims.text: Corrections that exposed participants to novel misinformation did not lead to stronger misconceptions compared to a control group never exposed to the false claims or corrections.
claims.quote: Corrections that exposed participants to novel misinformation did not lead to stronger misconceptions compared to a control group never exposed to the false claims or corrections.

claims.text: Implied misinformation is more resistant to correction than explicit misinformation, even when the correction is paired with an alternative explanation.
claims.quote: Experiment 2 showed that implied misinformation was more resistant to correction than explicit misinformation, even when the correction was paired with an alternative explanation.

claims.text: Continued influence remains for negative misinformation, but it reverses for corrected positive information, causing people to have more negative attitudes towards the hospital than before.
claims.quote: But whereas some persuasive impact remained for corrected negative misinformation (a continued influence effect), it reversed for corrected positive information, causing people to have more negative attitudes towards the hospital than before exposure to any information (a backfire effect).

claims.text: Correction does not entirely eliminate the effect of misinformation (r = –.05, p = .045).
claims.quote: Aggregation of results from 32 studies ( N = 6,527) revealed that, on average, correction does not entirely eliminate the effect of misinformation ( r = –.05, p = .045).

claims.text: Corrections are less effective if the misinformation was attributed to a credible source, repeated multiple times, or if there was a time lag.
claims.quote: Corrections are less effective if the misinformation was attributed to a credible source, the misinformation has been repeated multiple times prior to correction, or when there was a time lag between the delivery of the misinformation and the correction.

verdict: The evidence confirms that misinformation persists after correction, though the strength of this persistence depends on the type of misinformation and the delivery of the correction.
caveat: The effectiveness of corrections is highly dependent on specific variables like the source of the information, the time lag, and whether the misinformation was explicit or implied.
caption:
A correction does not always erase the first impression.

Research shows that misinformation persists after debunking, especially when it is implied or negative. The effectiveness of a correction depends on the source, the time lag, and the nature of the claim.

Have you ever felt a lingering doubt after reading a fact-check?
